The risk assessment Uteratin’e is voluminous and any selective listing of 
references would inevitably be distorted and incomplete. For a lucid and still 
influential account of quantitative risk assessment for chemical carcinogens, 
and a penetrating discussion of its numerous uncertainties, see National 
Research Council, Risk Assessment in the Federal Government: Managing the 
Process (1983). A more recent treatment of the process is National Research 
Council, Science and Decisions: Advancing Risk Assessment (2009).
For many of these reasons, judicial review of such risk assessments poses 
challenges. See Industrial Union Department, AFL-CIO v. Hodgson, 499 F.2d 
467, 473—76 (D.C. Cir. 1974) (noting that, where “some of the questions 
involved in the promulgation of these standards are on the frontiers of 
scientific knowledge, and consequently as to them insuf&cient data is presently 
available to make a fully informed factual determination,” “[d]ecision making 
must in that circumstance depend to a greater extent upon policy judgments 
and less upon purely factual analysis”); American Petroleum Inst. v. EPA, 661 
F.2d 340, 349 (5th Cir. 1981) (reasoning that an agency “is entitled to exercise 
its discretion, but only so far and no further; and its decision need not be ideal 
or even, perhaps, correct so long as not ‘arbitrary’ or ‘capricious’ and so long as 
the agency gave at least minimal consideration to the relevant facts as 
contained in the record”).
b. Agency Interpretation of Regulations
Agencies do not only have occasion to construe statutory text. They 
also may interpret a wide variety of other types of documents—^including 
the Constitution, government contracts with private parties, and executive 
orders. Should courts employ the same standard of review for agency 
statutory interpretation when judging agency interpretations of such 
texts? Or should courts adopt a different standard of review for different 
types of documents?
The question of the appropriate standard of review arises with 
frequency in the specific context of agency interpretations of their own 
ambiguous regulations. There, courts must ask whether agencies receive 
some weight for their interpretations of regulations that agency personnel 
have presumably written. To date, the Court has followed an approach 
established by two of its precedents, Bowles v. Seminole Rock & Sand Co., 
325 U.S. 410 (1945), and Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452 (1997). The two 
cases have come to represent a form of deference interchangeably referred 
to as “Seminole Rock deference” or “Auer deference.”
